title: The history of the snowflake
tagline: From a Chinese scholar's six-pointed flowers to cellular models on a hex grid, 2,000 years of asking why snow has six arms.
intro: People noticed the six-fold shape of snow long ago. Kepler asked why, microscopes and cameras showed the detail, and a Japanese lab finally grew crystals on demand. Today models on a computer can grow six matching arms from one simple rule.

eras.name: Seeing six corners
eras.summary: Scholars noticed the six points. Kepler and Descartes tried to explain them, and Hooke looked closer.

eras.name: Drawing and photographing
eras.summary: Whalers, lords and farmers drew and then photographed thousands of crystals.

eras.name: Growing snow in the lab
eras.summary: In Hokkaido, Nakaya grew crystals on demand and mapped their shapes.

eras.name: Models and myths
eras.summary: Scientists weighed the no-two-alike saying and built models that grow flakes in code.

events.title: "Snow flowers are six-pointed"
events.text: The Chinese scholar Han Ying wrote that plant flowers usually have five points, but snow flowers always have six. It is the earliest known account of the snowflake's six-fold shape.
events.why: It shows that the six-fold puzzle is more than two thousand years old.

events.title: A poet calls snowflakes six-petalled
events.text: The poet Hsiao Tung described snowflakes as six-petalled. The page that records this gives no more precise date.
events.why: The six-petal idea was already part of how people spoke about snow.

events.title: A bishop lists snow shapes
events.text: The Scandinavian bishop Olaus Magnus gave the first known European reference to snow crystal shapes, such as crescents and arrows. The source notes it hardly counts as a scientific first.
events.why: Europeans began writing about the varied shapes of snow.

events.title: Harriot spots the six-fold symmetry
events.text: Thomas Harriot correctly noted the six-fold symmetry of snow crystals, according to the SnowCrystals.com history.
events.why: An early scientific observation of the symmetry that Kepler would try to explain.

events.title: Kepler asks why snow has six corners
events.text: Kepler wrote a short New Year's gift for his patron asking why snowflakes have six points. He compared the shape to tightly packed spheres and honeycomb cells. He found no firm answer and ended the essay open.
events.why: It was the first scientific attempt to explain the symmetry, and an early step toward crystallography.

events.title: Descartes describes snow crystals in detail
events.text: In Les Météores, Descartes gave a detailed account based on his own observations of snow, including capped columns and unusual twelve-rayed stars. His drawings were weaker than his words. He could not explain the six-fold symmetry.
events.why: It was the first detailed study of snow crystal structure.

events.title: Hooke draws snowflakes under a microscope
events.text: In Micrographia, Hooke published engravings of magnified snowflakes (Plate 8). They are stylised, but they are among the first magnified pictures of snow.
events.why: The microscope showed that snow has fine structure, not just a vague star shape.

events.title: Scoresby draws snow crystals at sea
events.text: The whaling captain William Scoresby Jr. drew snowflakes in the Arctic and published the drawings in An Account of the Arctic Regions. Sketches found in 2024 at the Whitby Museum show how he made them.
events.why: It gave readers a catalogue of crystal forms, drawn from real observation.

events.title: Doi Toshitsura publishes Sekka zusetsu
events.text: A Japanese lord, Doi Toshitsura, drew 86 snow crystals he had seen through a microscope. He published them in 1832 as Sekka zusetsu, along with 12 figures borrowed from a Dutch book.
events.why: It is an outstanding early catalogue of snow crystal shapes, made outside Europe.

events.title: Flögel photographs snow crystals
events.text: The University of Regensburg library page says Johann Flögel photographed snow crystals on 1 February 1879, which would make him earlier than Wilson Bentley.
events.why: It shows that Bentley's fame was earned by quantity and persistence, not by being first.

events.title: Bentley takes his first snow crystal photograph
events.text: A Vermont farmer, Wilson Bentley, fixed a camera to a microscope and photographed a snow crystal. He went on to photograph well over 5,000.
events.why: His photographs made the beauty and variety of snow crystals known to the public.

events.title: Bentley: "no one design was ever repeated"
events.text: In a 1925 report, Bentley wrote that every crystal was a masterpiece of design and no design was ever repeated. This is the source of the saying that no two snowflakes are alike.
events.why: The saying became a popular myth, but he only reported what he had photographed.

events.title: Bentley and Humphreys publish Snow Crystals
events.who: Wilson A. Bentley and W. J. Humphreys
events.text: The book Snow Crystals, with Bentley's photographs, came out in November 1931. Bentley died a few weeks later, on 23 December, at his family farm.
events.why: It preserved his life's work for scientists and the public.

events.title: Nakaya opens a low temperature laboratory
events.text: Ukichiro Nakaya, who had joined Hokkaido University in 1930, opened a Low Temperature Science Laboratory in 1935 to study snow in the lab.
events.why: It was a place where snow crystals could be grown and studied on demand.

events.title: The first artificial snow crystal
events.text: Nakaya grew the first artificial snow crystal, on a single rabbit hair in cold, humid air. It showed that crystals could be grown under control.
events.why: Controlled experiments could finally show how conditions set the shape.

events.title: The Nakaya diagram
events.text: Nakaya and his collaborators grew crystals at different temperatures and humidities and found that shape flips between plates, columns and needles as temperature changes. The result is called the Nakaya or morphology diagram.
events.why: It turned the question of why snowflakes differ into a map you can read.

events.title: Snow Crystals: Natural and Artificial
events.text: Nakaya's book summarising his work was published by Harvard University Press. In it, he describes snow crystals as letters sent from heaven.
events.why: It took Japanese snow research to an international audience.

events.title: Nancy Knight teaches in Hokkaido
events.text: Nancy Knight, later a snow and ice scientist at NCAR, spent about two years at Hokkaido University in the mid-1960s. There she taught English and helped Japanese scientists to prepare their papers in English.
events.why: It links the Japanese snow school to later American work.

events.title: Magono and Lee classify natural snow crystals
events.who: Choji Magono and Chung Woo Lee
events.text: Magono and Lee published a meteorological classification of natural snow crystals in the Journal of the Faculty of Science at Hokkaido University. Their scheme lists about 80 shapes in eight main groups.
events.why: It gave scientists shared names for snow crystal types.

events.title: "No Two Alike?"
events.text: Nancy Knight published a paper in the Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society about two nearly matching hollow crystals from a Wisconsin storm. She did not say they were identical, but many people took the title that way. Libbrecht later grew lab twins that are close, not exact.
events.why: It showed how alike and identical get mixed up, and put a figure on the old myth.

events.title: Reiter publishes a cellular model of snow growth
events.text: Clifford Reiter, at Lafayette College, published a simple two-parameter cellular automaton on a hexagonal grid. It makes plates, stars and especially realistic dendrites.
events.why: Even a very simple rule can grow flakes with six matching arms.

events.title: Libbrecht reviews the physics of snow crystals
events.text: Libbrecht's review in Reports on Progress in Physics treats snow crystals as a case study in growth from vapour. It covers branching, surface structure and the way shape changes with temperature.
events.why: It brought snow crystal growth into the mainstream of crystal physics.

events.title: Gravner and Griffeath model snow in 3D
events.text: Gravner and Griffeath posted a three-dimensional cellular model, mixing vapour diffusion, direction-dependent attachment and a semi-liquid boundary layer. Their virtual crystals look like many real flakes.
events.why: It showed that thickness and ribbing can be modelled too, not just flat outlines.

events.title: Libbrecht proposes why habit flips with temperature
events.text: Libbrecht described a mechanism combining surface melting and impurities as a candidate explanation for the flip between plates and columns, which he called a 60-year-old mystery. He said that more work is needed.
events.why: The reason shape flips with temperature is still being researched.

events.title: Scoresby's working sketches found
events.text: A researcher at Whitby Museum reported a folded sheet of Scoresby's sketches of snowflake segments, found in the museum's archive. Pencil marks link them to May 1817 log entries and to drawings in his 1820 book.
events.why: Archives can still turn up how the first snow catalogues were made.

Kepler's snowflake essay was a New Year's gift to a friend and patron.
Nakaya grew his first artificial crystal on a rabbit hair.
Reiter's model has no random numbers, so the same settings always grow the same flake.
